title: Learning and Motivational Impact of Game-Based Learning: Comparing Face-To-Face and Online Formats on Computer Science Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teacher-authored educational video games are effective for learning and motivation in computer science education, and whether their effectiveness differs when the game is used face-to-face versus online. The authors frame the problem around the need for motivating instructional methods in computer science, where dropout rates can be high, and around the practical difficulty teachers face in finding or creating games aligned with course objectives.

The intervention studied is a teacher-authored educational video game created with the SGAME authoring tool and embedded learning objects built with ViSH Editor. The game is based on Flappy Bird mechanics: students play while periodically encountering integrated learning objects containing self-grading multiple-choice questions and short explanatory content about software design concepts. Students had to answer correctly to continue, making the learning and gameplay tightly interwoven.

The study was conducted in a software engineering fundamentals course at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid with 321 undergraduate computer science students. One cohort (104 students) completed the activity online during the COVID-19 period, and another cohort (217 students) completed it face-to-face in a later academic year. Pre-test/post-test data and a questionnaire were used to measure learning gains, motivation, usability, and perceptions. Results showed significant knowledge gains in both formats, similar learning effectiveness across formats, and generally positive student perceptions. The face-to-face format produced somewhat more favorable ratings for fun, overall opinion, future use, and preference over traditional materials, but online implementation was also effective and usable. The paper concludes that teacher-authored educational video games can support both learning and motivation in computer science classes, regardless of delivery mode, while face-to-face settings may yield slightly stronger subjective enjoyment.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental comparative study with a fairly large sample (n=321), clear pre/post measures, and statistical testing, but it is not randomized and compares different cohorts across academic years. That creates selection and time-related confounds, so it falls short of blue-tier evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention showed medium-to-large gains on academic outcomes within both groups (d=0.71 and d=0.79), which meets the threshold for blue impact. The motivational benefits were also consistently positive, though some between-format differences were modest.

interventions.use_case: teacher-authored educational video game for software design learning, implemented as a Flappy Bird-style game with embedded SCORM-compliant learning objects and self-grading multiple-choice questions

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-authored educational video games improved knowledge acquisition in both formats. Pre- to post-test gains were statistically significant for both groups (face-to-face n=217, d=0.71; online n=104, d=0.79), with post-test means of 7.76 vs 7.51 and learning gains of 1.73 vs 1.82 on a 0-10 scale. Between-group differences in learning gains were negligible and not significant (d=0.05), indicating similar academic effectiveness across formats.
finding.measure: Pre-test and post-test scores on 10 multiple-choice questions about basic principles of software design; learning gains (post-test minus pre-test)
finding.std_deviation: Pre-test SD=1.77/1.57; Post-test SD=1.66/1.68; Gain SD=1.79/2.03

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high motivation, engagement, and enjoyment from the game in both formats. Questionnaire ratings were strong for engagement/motivation (item 5: M=4.37 face-to-face vs 4.23 online) and fun (item 6: M=4.38 vs 4.20), with a statistically significant advantage for face-to-face on fun (d=0.20) and overall opinion (item 1: d=0.36). Overall average ratings were 4.32 face-to-face and 4.16 online on a 5-point scale.
finding.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire items on overall opinion, learning effectiveness, engagement/motivation, fun, future use, and preference over traditional materials
finding.effect_size: overall opinion d=0.36; learning effectiveness d=0.25; fun d=0.20; future use d=0.29; preference over traditional materials d=0.39
finding.std_deviation: Item SDs ranged from 0.55 to 1.35 across groups
